<div class="site-note">
<p>This is George Long&#x27;s English translation (London, 1890), taken unaltered from the Perseus Digital Library and used here under a Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 licence. Long&#x27;s own footnotes are kept, at the foot of each discourse.</p>
<p>The <i>Discourses</i> are the lessons Epictetus, a freed slave and Stoic teacher, gave at Nicopolis. His pupil Arrian put them into writing. Four of the original eight books survive. The theme is always the same, approached from every angle: what is in our power and what is not, and what freedom is. Judgement, impulse, desire, and aversion are in our power; the body, possessions, reputation, and public office are not. On this distinction Epictetus builds a demanding, yet deeply human, conception of freedom.</p>
</div>

<div class="site-usage">The three editions — Italian, English and Greek — have the same pages: the flags at the top move between them without leaving the discourse.</div>
